Selected work

SECURITALY · APR 2026 – PRESENT

The GEO plugins came first — a self-directed project that led to a meeting proposing further AI initiatives, and from there, conversations with the marketing and sales teams about what was actually costing them time. Six systems followed, some small, some not.

GEO infrastructure — an AI-search visibility layer

AI INFRASTRUCTURE · ORGANIC GROWTH
AI crawlers (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot, Amazonbot) were reading every site — completely untracked, with zero optimization for how they extract and cite content.

The first thing I built at Securitaly. The idea was simple to state and less simple to build: the way Yoast handles SEO, I wanted something that handled GEO. I designed and shipped five custom plugins — one per brand, across PrestaShop 1.7, PrestaShop 8, and WordPress — each tracking which AI bots and crawlers visit the site and which pages they read most. Connected to the Claude API, the same plugin auto-generates GEO content directly on each product page — AI Page Summaries and FAQs written for how generative engines extract and cite answers — alongside structured data and an llms.txt entry point for crawlers.

Every plugin ships under a constraint most engineers never face: there's no staging environment. Every release goes straight to a live storefront, which pushed me toward strict defensive habits — ASCII-only output, every hook wrapped in try/catch, a brace-balance check before anything deploys.

Securitaly HQ — the internal RevOps platform

PLATFORM · FLAGSHIP BUILD
Marketing could see newsletter opens and clicks in Brevo — but had no way to know what happened after: did people visit the site, did they buy.

After the plugins, I met with the marketing and then the sales team to find out what was actually costing them time. A narrow ask came out of that: give marketing real visibility into how their newsletters were performing beyond Brevo's own numbers. That scope kept growing. I designed and built an internal analytics and operations platform from scratch, end to end — data pipeline, database schema, and dashboard. It now unifies GEO/AI-visibility monitoring, SEO performance with year-over-year comparison, email marketing analytics with full-funnel tracking, conversion attribution by traffic source, and an AI datasheet generator across seven brands, for a company that previously had no consolidated view of any of it.

Started as a no-code prototype (Make.com + Google Sheets + Lovable) to validate the concept fast, then rebuilt as a modular Python pipeline on GitHub Actions writing to a Postgres database, once the no-code version hit its operation caps and error-handling limits. The frontend stayed untouched through the rebuild — the team's experience never broke.

Newsletter & campaign attribution

ATTRIBUTION · MARKETING OPS
Email campaigns went out across seven brands with no shared view of what actually worked — and no link to revenue.

Built the join that didn't exist: connecting Brevo (email send data) to GA4 (on-site behavior and purchases) using utm_id as the reliable join key. The pipeline fetches every campaign, detects its brand from the naming pattern, pulls matching GA4 session and revenue data, and deduplicates on upsert so each campaign stays a single, current row.

The result: a single funnel view per campaign — sent → delivered → opened → clicked → session → purchase — replacing what used to require manually pulling reports from three separate tools.

Conversion path & revenue visibility

ATTRIBUTION · FUNNEL TRACKING
For the B2B brands, almost every sale starts with a contact form — but nobody could see what a lead looked at before filling it in.

Added GA4 event tracking into the pipeline to reconstruct the path to conversion: which landing pages and which traffic source or medium actually drive form submissions ("Contacted") and purchases ("Sold"), per brand — split out from the AI-bot and crawler traffic the GEO layer also tracks, so the team isn't reading bot noise as real visitor behavior. The same pipeline now surfaces brand-level sales — transactions, revenue, sessions — with a year-over-year comparison the team never had in one place before.

AI datasheet generator for sales

AUTOMATION · SALES ENABLEMENT
Producing one product datasheet — translating raw specs, often from Chinese suppliers, into a formatted PDF — took the sales team a lot of back-and-forth with marketing.

Built to close a friction point between sales and marketing: sales works through a guided, three-step form inside the dashboard — product identity, technical specs (pasted, typed, or uploaded as a PDF, in any language), and finally the AI-assisted content for the sheet itself. A Supabase Edge Function proxies the request to the Claude API. The template style was designed together with the marketing and design team, so every generated datasheet is on-brand by default rather than something sales has to format by hand.

Output is a print-ready, brand-consistent datasheet with imagery, specs, and comparison tables — reviewed and approved by a person before it ever reaches a customer.

Shared AI prompt library

ENABLEMENT · KNOWLEDGE OPS
Marketing and sales kept rebuilding the same prompts from scratch, for tasks they repeated every week or month.

Not everything worth building is a pipeline. After hearing the same complaint from a few different people, I put together a shared library on Google Drive — prompts organized by brand and by department, ready to reuse for recurring work like translations, product copy, and social captions, instead of everyone starting from a blank page each time.
